title: Aid contraction turns refugee integration into a shared jobs, food-security, and local-capacity problem
source_unit: World Bank, As Aid Shrinks, Jobs Become Central to Self-reliance for Host Communities and Refugees in Kenya; based on the Kenya Longitudinal Socioeconomic Study under KAP-FD
geography: Kenya, with evidence from refugee and host communities in Kakuma, Kalobeyei, Dadaab, Turkana, Garissa, and urban settings; national refugee and asylum-seeker context

observations.period: 2022-2024; two-wave panel evidence summarized by the World Bank

denominator.unit: survey waves following the same refugee and host households over time

population_context.unit: refugees and asylum seekers hosted by Kenya as of April 2026

multidimensional_poverty.value: more than four out of five refugees in Kakuma, Kalobeyei, and Dadaab are multidimensionally poor across education, employment, housing, water, and nutrition

aid_revenue_dependence.unit: percent approximate share of total revenue accounted for by aid among camp-based refugees in 2024

local_market_transmission.value: ration cuts and suspended vouchers reduced refugee incomes and demand in camp economies, affecting host livelihoods tied to trade, services, and casual work

observations.method: World Bank feature synthesis of two waves of a longitudinal socioeconomic panel produced with UNHCR and the Center for Effective Global Action, supplemented by program and administrative context.
observations.uncertainty: The feature reports selected panel findings and contextual interpretation; the survey predates the deepest aid cuts described after late 2024, and results from these settings should not be generalized to all refugee-hosting economies.
observations.subgroup: Refugees in camps and urban areas, host communities in Turkana and Garissa, children, women with care responsibilities, and households dependent on aid or thin local labor markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aid contraction can create pressure for self-reliance, but without legal work access, mobility, investment, and local public capacity, it may deepen poverty rather than produce independent livelihoods.

observations.period: 2022-2024; refugee and host labor-market changes between panel waves

denominator.unit: panel waves used for employment and inactivity comparison

camp_refugee_employment.unit: reported employment share change among camp-based refugees

urban_refugee_employment.unit: reported employment share change among urban refugees

camp_inactivity.unit: percent inactivity among camp-based refugees in the later wave

job_availability_constraint.unit: percent of camp-based refugees citing lack of available jobs, up from 41%

observations.method: Longitudinal comparison of refugee and host labor-market indicators as summarized in the World Bank feature.
observations.uncertainty: Employment shares and inactivity are setting-specific and do not by themselves distinguish legal restrictions, demand collapse, seasonality, skills mismatch, health, care, or measurement changes.
observations.subgroup: Camp-based refugees, urban refugees, camp-adjacent host communities, women facing care and mobility constraints, and workers in local trade, services, agriculture, and casual work.
observations.counterinterpretation: A fall in measured employment may conceal informal, intermittent, or unreported work; nevertheless the reported job-availability response and high inactivity indicate weak absorptive capacity rather than simple unwillingness to work.

observations.period: 2022-2024; formal labor-market access and gendered constraints

denominator.unit: Kenya refugee labor-market access context described in the panel study summary

work_permit_access.unit: percent approximate share of refugees holding a work permit in the first survey wave

mobility_barrier.value: administrative hurdles and mobility restrictions constrain formal labor-market entry

women_constraints.value: care responsibilities, limited mobility, weak job availability, and lack of childcare or safe work opportunities compound women’s exclusion

integration_boundary.value: integrated settlements cannot produce self-reliance without actual work and mobility access

observations.method: Policy and labor-market interpretation of panel evidence within Kenya’s shift from encampment toward integrated settlements under the Shirika Plan.
observations.uncertainty: The feature does not estimate the causal contribution of each legal, mobility, childcare, or investment barrier or evaluate the Shirika Plan’s implementation outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Refugees seeking formal work, women and caregivers, host-community workers in lagging regions, employers, local governments, and services dependent on aid-supported economies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Legal work authorization is necessary but not sufficient: thin local demand, transport, skills, safety, care infrastructure, capital, and employer willingness also shape realized opportunity.

observations.period: 2024; household coping under aid, price, and climate pressure

denominator.unit: later panel-wave camp-household coping context reported by the World Bank

food_reduction.unit: percent of camp households reporting reduced food consumption

food_credit.unit: percent of camp households relying on credit to buy food

shock_exposure.value: food-price pressure, excessive rainfall, flooding, damaged infrastructure, and weak agricultural or livestock livelihoods

wellbeing_pressure.value: rising stress and anxiety undermine coping and the ability to invest in future livelihoods

service_gap.value: nutrition-service coverage gaps compound sustained nutritional stress

observations.method: Panel-based household coping indicators and contextual reporting on food prices, climate shocks, nutrition, and mental-health pressure.
observations.uncertainty: The feature reports coping prevalence without establishing which shock or policy lever caused each household response; negative coping is an indicator of stress, not a complete measure of welfare.
observations.subgroup: Camp households, children, host communities reliant on agriculture and livestock, households with food insecurity, and people exposed to climate and aid shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit, ration changes, migration, informal work, remittances, and community support may buffer some households, but the source does not estimate their relative protective effects.

related_sources.claim: Associated World Bank, UNHCR, and CEGA report: Building Evidence to Enhance the Welfare of Refugees and Host Communities in Kenya: Insights from Two Waves of the Kenya Longitudinal Socioeconomic Study.
UNHCR Kenya operational data context for refugees and asylum seekers.

boundary: This record adds a place-based displacement-to-work-and-household-security route. It is not a universal refugee-outcome estimate, a causal evaluation of the Shirika Plan, a complete labor-market census, or proof that jobs alone resolve poverty, social cohesion, gendered care constraints, food insecurity, or public-service capacity.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank feature reviewed for two-wave panel design, refugee population context, multidimensional poverty, aid dependence, employment changes, work-permit access, gendered constraints, food coping, climate shocks, and the integration-to-jobs implementation condition.
